title: Relay Architectures and Ecological Strategies of Quorum Sensing Effects on Microbial Interactions
content:
Quorum‐sensing activity in one population affects neighbouring populations through direct signal perception, QS‐regulated chemical effectors, or host‐ or environment‐mediated relays. Across distinct habitats, these relay architectures are associated with ecological strategies ranging from shared signal accessibility and reciprocal responsiveness to resource monopolization, niche restructuring, and associational resistance.

ABSTRACT
Microbial communities assemble in heterogeneous habitats, where quorum sensing (QS) influences interactions beyond signalling populations. Yet QS studies are commonly organized by signal type, circuit, or phenotype, obscuring the routes by which a QS event reaches neighbouring populations and why they prevail in particular settings. This Review synthesizes evidence from host‐associated, terrestrial, marine, and aquatic systems to develop a two‐dimensional framework for QS‐mediated ecological effects. The framework distinguishes three relay architectures by which QS activity in one population affects another: direct perception of the source signal, exposure to a QS‐regulated chemical effector, or response to a QS‐associated change in a shared host or environment. It then identifies the ecological strategies that these architectures can support, including shared signal accessibility, reciprocal coordination, asymmetric cue responsiveness, resource monopolization, and competitive or community restructuring. Across habitats, spatial structure, resource accessibility, host‐associated conditions, and temporal variability shape which relay architectures are feasible and the ecological consequences they generate. The framework positions QS as a context‐dependent process through which population‐state sensing is translated into neighbour responses, changes in habitat conditions, and community assembly. It establishes testable expectations for predicting which QS‐mediated interactions arise in a habitat and for designing interventions that steer microbiome function.

title: What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
content:
What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
Fabio Turco, Iris Feigenwinter, Lorenz Allemann, Lukas Hörtnagl, Frank Liebisch, and Nina Buchmann
Biogeosciences, 23, 7151–7182, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7151-2026, 2026
Fertilized cropland is a major source of nitrous oxide, but when and why it is emitted within a season is still poorly known. We measured it continuously above a Swiss winter wheat field for a year. Emissions exceeded those typical for wheat, and machine learning showed they peaked during crop establishment and early spring, when wet soil and large amounts of nitrogen met low plant uptake. Vigorous growth lowered emissions, so matching nitrogen supply to plant demand is a promising lever.

title: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
content:
Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
Chueh-Chen Tung, Moritz Holtappels, Alexa Wrede, Male Köster, Lasse Sander, Jan Beermann, Vera Sidorenko, and Lars Gutow
Biogeosciences, 23, 7129–7150, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7129-2026, 2026
Using 171 taxa from 50 stations in the southeastern North Sea, we show that environmental gradients structure benthic macrofaunal communities and their traits. Deeper communities had higher bioturbation and bioirrigation, whereas shallow communities showed greater respiration and secondary production. Environmental gradients also shifted biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships, highlighting macrofaunal control of carbon sequestration–related processes in shelf sea sediments.

title: Paleochannels Facilitate Large‐Scale Submarine Groundwater Discharge on the Southwestern East China Sea Shelf
content:
Abstract
In addition to surface runoff, coastal seas receive water and nutrients via subsurface pathways, including submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) at the meter‐to‐kilometer scale and porewater exchange (PEX) at the centimeter scale. Partitioning SGD and PEX fluxes is important for understanding their biogeochemical impacts, particularly on continental margins. Here, we integrated field data and a dual‐radium (224Ra and 226Ra) mass balance model to decipher the magnitude, relative contributions, and potential drivers of SGD and PEX on the southwestern East China Sea shelf during a spring red tide period. Constrained by Monte Carlo simulations, the estimated SGD flux north of 26°N was 18 (7.7–42) cm d−1, ∼2 times the PEX flux of 9.0 (4.1–20) cm d−1. By contrast, SGD and PEX fluxes south of 26°N were comparable. Volumetrically, total benthic advective water flow was 2.6 (1.1–6.0) × 109 m3 d−1, equivalent to ∼15 times the local river discharge. In the northern region, extensive relict paleochannel systems beneath the seabed serve as preferential conduits for long‐distance SGD transport to the coastal ocean, as evidenced by existing geomorphological and geophysical mappings from shallow seismic profiles. Our findings underscore that large‐scale SGD through these paleochannels represents a critical yet overlooked pathway, potentially driving biogeochemical processes in coastal waters.

title: Host‐Associated Differentiation in a Parasitoid Wasp Connected to Venom‐Related but Not Chemosensory Genes
content:
ABSTRACT
The mechanisms driving the megadiversity of parasitic wasps remain a central question in evolutionary ecology. To investigate the genomic architecture underlying host‐associated differentiation in parasitic wasps, we generated a de novo genome assembly and performed whole‐genome re‐sequencing of 17 populations of the parasitoid wasp Asecodes parviclava (Eulophidae) across a latitudinal gradient and multiple Galerucella host species. Despite panmixia in host populations, we identified three genetically differentiated wasp lineages, with the most profound divergence separating Galerucella tenella‐associated wasps from other populations. Locus‐specific scans revealed that selection acts highly asymmetrically. We detected significant differentiation and copy‐number expansion clustered within venom‐related gene families, contrasting sharply with a near‐complete lack of divergence in chemosensory genes. This decoupled evolution suggests that host finding may rely on behavioural plasticity, whereas physiological compatibility is genetically hard‐wired via multi‐layered immune‐suppression mechanisms. Finally, asymmetrical gene flow in northern populations demonstrates that fine‐scale habitat overlap creates ecological connectivity without eroding specialized lineages, as intense host‐mediated selection purges maladapted hybrids. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that physiological barriers, rather than behavioural recognition, may maintain specialized parasitoid lineages, providing new insights into the genomic basis of speciation with gene flow in specialized natural enemies.

title: Limited Lifetime Costs of Inbreeding in a Large Wild Population of Superb Fairy‐Wrens
content:
ABSTRACT
Inbreeding depression can have major negative effects on both individual fitness and population performance. The impact of inbreeding depression in wild populations remains poorly understood, and our knowledge is primarily based on estimations in insular populations with limited dispersal, which has been predicted to enhance the capacity for outcrossing. Limited migration and small population sizes, which make insular and endangered populations tractable models for fieldwork, often experience low genetic variation and may be subject to stronger inbreeding effects. Estimating inbreeding effects is difficult in many populations because pedigrees of migrants are unknown. Genomic data offer methods to estimate realised inbreeding even in migrants. Here, we apply genomic methods to a superb fairy‐wren (Malurus cyaneus) population that has been subject to detailed study of fitness variation over three decades. The population has sex‐biased dispersal, resulting in many immigrant females. We use genomic inbreeding estimates to explicitly test for inbreeding depression across several key components of individual fitness, including nestling condition, juvenile survival and adult traits. Genomic methods were able to recover previous pedigree‐based findings of inbreeding depression in early nestling condition and additionally identified some evidence for inbreeding depression in fledgling but not juvenile mortality. The only adult fitness trait affected, male extra‐pair paternity, is highly variable and under strong sexual selection. Our findings suggest that natural populations experiencing high effective population sizes and regular dispersal might be less affected by inbreeding depression than previously assumed based on studies of often insular and smaller populations.

title: Global change threatens the biodiversity of cold regions: Current knowledge and priorities for further research
content:
Abstract
Cold regions are among the most pristine areas remaining globally, hosting unique fauna and flora. Historically, these regions have often been refugia from land‐use change, resource exploitation, and pollution, but climate warming and biological invasions increasingly constitute profound threats. Focusing on terrestrial plant and invertebrate species, we provide an overview of the impacts of climate change and biological invasions on the biodiversity of cold regions, from the individual to the species level, and discuss pervasive challenges to understanding and managing these impacts. In particular, we explore the consequences of climate change and biological invasions in the contexts of individual physiology, population dynamics, and species redistribution. We suggest new research avenues by identifying priorities for future studies on plants and invertebrates of cold regions in the context of concurrent climate change and biological invasion.

title: Sparse neuronal C4 elevation induces network-wide transcriptomic and lipid-droplet remodeling in the cortical microenvironment
content:
by Marta Sánchez-Carbonell, Sonia Bolshakova, Juan E. Ávila-Pagán, Yaseer A. Sabir, Clay Griffin-Derr, Dominik G. Stich, Sofia V. Cieslewicz, Sheyla Esther Carmen Sifuentes, Rhushikesh A. Phadke, Alison Brack, Anna Hasche-Kluender, Paige Caley, Caroline Dias, Alberto Cruz-Martín

The complement component C4 regulates synaptic refinement and plasticity in the brain and has been implicated in multiple neurological and psychiatric disorders, with especially strong genetic evidence linking elevated C4A expression to schizophrenia. However, it remains unclear whether localized C4 elevation in a small neuronal population is sufficient to reshape broader cortical gene-regulatory programs and cellular phenotypes. To address this question, we overexpressed mouse C4 in approximately 2% of prefrontal cortical neurons using in utero electroporation and performed bulk RNA sequencing on microdissected prefrontal cortex. Despite the sparse manipulation, C4-OE was associated with broad transcriptional remodeling across tissue composed predominantly of untransfected cells, including coordinated changes in cholesterol biosynthesis, axon- and synaptic-associated programs, vascular/ECM pathways, and immune- and stress-related responses. Comparison with a schizophrenia synaptic proteomic dataset identified limited global correspondence but selective gene- and pathway-level overlap in specific molecular programs. Reference-based projection of directional DEG signatures onto a cortical single-cell transcriptomic reference further identified cell-type-associated structure, including prominent astrocyte- and vascular-associated axes and distinct lipid/metabolic, vascular/endothelial–interferon-associated, and immune/stress correlation domains. Spatial validation with MFISH showed increased Hmgcr expression in neighboring GFP-negative cells, while PLIN2 imaging revealed increased DAPI-associated/perinuclear lipid-droplet burden within the local C4-OE field. Together, these findings support a model in which sparse neuronal C4 elevation is associated with broader remodeling of the local cortical environment, including a non-cell-autonomous component involving neighboring-cell lipid-associated responses. These results expand the interpretation of C4 risk biology beyond synapse elimination alone and suggest that focal immune-gene dysregulation can engage lipid-homeostatic, stress-related, and cell-type-associated transcriptional programs relevant to cortical circuit vulnerability.

title: Identification of letters distorted by physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling
content:
by Raffles Xingqi Zhu, Alex S. Baldwin

In the geniculostriate pathway of the human visual system, neuronal projections carry signals from a particular retinal locus in parallel from one anatomical area to the next. Imprecision in the fidelity of these projections would place constraints on the ability of the system to perform tasks requiring positional information. We investigated the impact that “spatial scrambling” between stages would have on visual performance. We consider two stages in a simple canonical model of the early visual cortex where scrambling might occur: either the input to the first orientation-tuned mechanisms (analogous to V1 simple cells), or the output from those mechanisms. These are referred as “subcortical” (SCS) and “cortical scrambling” (CS). We developed a wavelet decomposition and resynthesis algorithm to mimic these effects, and measured human performance in letter identification affected by the two types of scrambling. Our results showed SCS and CS have distinguishable effects on both perceived noisiness of letters and letter identification threshold. Comparing human performance against a suite of pre-trained and custom convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that were trained on the scrambled stimuli, relative efficiency (calculated from the ratio of human:CNN thresholds) is higher for CS than SCS. However, in modelling human inefficiency by reducing the proportion of wavelets available to the CNNs, humans are less efficient in CS than SCS. These differences in efficiencies show humans are better at processing orientation redundant stimuli (CS) than orientation noisy stimuli (SCS). We hypothesize this reflects differences in integration properties at the input and output stages of simple cells in the cortex.

title: Latent encoding of movement in primary visual cortex
content:
by Hannah Germaine, Isaiah Choi, Stephen D. Van Hooser, Jérôme Ribot, Jonathan David Touboul

Neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) are classically thought to encode spatial features of visual stimuli through simple population codes: each neuron exhibits a preferred orientation and preferred spatial frequency, both of which remaining invariant to other aspects of the visual stimulus. Here, we show that this simple rule does not apply to the representation of major features of stimulus motion, including stimulus direction and temporal frequency (TF). We collected an extensive dataset of cat V1 responses to stimuli covarying in orientation, direction, spatial frequency, and TF to assess the extent of motion selectivity. We show that preferred TF is mostly uniform across the cortical surface. Yet, in over half of V1, the preferred direction is reversed with changing stimulus TF, revealing four distinct map motifs embedded in V1’s functional architecture. Similarly, despite the lack of spatial modulation for the preferred TF map and the lack of invariance for the preferred direction map, we found using convolutional neural networks that direction, TF and stimulus speed can be accurately decoded from V1 responses at all cortical locations. These findings suggest a latent encoding of information where subtle, spatially distributed modulations of V1 activity may convey fine information about stimulus motion, pointing to a novel primary sensory encoding mechanism despite complex co-variation of responses to multiple attributes across V1 neurons.

title: Understanding cell fate decisions with temporal attention
content:
by Florian Bürger, Martim Dias Gomes, Adrián E. Granada, Noémie Moreau, Katarzyna Bozek

Understanding non-genetic determinants of cell fate is critical for developing and improving cancer therapies, as genetically identical cells can exhibit divergent outcomes under the same treatment conditions. In this work, we present a deep learning approach for cell fate prediction from raw long-term live-cell recordings of cancer cell populations under chemotherapeutic treatment. Our Transformer model is trained to predict cell fate directly from raw image sequences, without relying on predefined morphological or molecular features. Beyond classification, we introduce a comprehensive explainability framework for interpreting the temporal and morphological cues guiding the model’s predictions. We demonstrate that prediction of cell outcomes is possible based on the video only, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.94 and an F1-score of 0.93. Attention and masking experiments further indicate that the signal predictive of the cell fate is not uniquely located in the final frames of a cell trajectory, as reliable predictions are possible up to 8 h before the event. Our analysis reveals distinct temporal distribution of predictive information in the mitotic and apoptotic sequences, as well as the role of cell morphology and p53 signaling in determining cell outcomes. Together, these findings demonstrate that attention-based temporal models enable accurate cell fate prediction while providing biologically interpretable insights into non-genetic determinants of cellular decision-making.

title: Antimony 3: Extending human-readable model definitions for SBML Level 3 Core and Packages
content:
by Adel Heydarabadipour, Lucian P. Smith, Joseph L. Hellerstein, Herbert M. Sauro

Antimony is a human-readable language for defining and sharing models developed by the systems biology community. It enables scientists to describe biochemical networks with a simple syntax, while supporting seamless conversion to and from the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) community standard. Since Antimony’s original release, both SBML and modeling practices have evolved significantly, creating a need to update Antimony to maintain its standards compliance and practical relevance. In this paper, we introduce Antimony 3, a comprehensive update that formalizes its cumulative improvements and extends its support for SBML Level 3 Core and Flux Balance Constraints (FBC), Distributions, Layout, and Render packages. Antimony 3 enables model specifications that combine kinetic reactions with flux balance analysis, represent uncertainty using probability distributions, add biological context through annotations, and define publication-ready visualizations, all within a unified plain-text format. Antimony 3 is delivered as a lightweight C/C++ library with a stable C API. It is available through official bindings for Python, Julia, and JavaScript/WebAssembly, as well as a cross-platform desktop GUI, which enables straightforward use across scripting environments, desktop applications, and browser-based tools. Antimony 3 is released as open-source software under the BSD 3-Clause License and is available at https://github.com/sys-bio/antimony.

title: Recombination shapes the dynamics of selective constraint in global populations of human gut bacteria
content:
by Zhiru Liu, Benjamin H. Good

The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) encodes important information about the selection pressures acting on protein-coding genes. In bacterial populations, dN/dS often declines with the sequence divergence between strains, but the mechanisms responsible for this broad empirical trend are still debated. Existing models have primarily focused on de novo mutations, overlooking the older genetic variants that are continually introduced through horizontal gene transfer and recombination. Here we introduce a phenomenological model of dN/dS in recombining populations of bacteria, which allows us to disentangle the effects of recombination among pairs of closely related strains. We find that clonally inherited regions of the genome exhibit consistently higher dN/dS ratios, and that the accumulation of recombined segments can quantitatively explain the majority of the decline in dN/dS. We use these observations to re-examine models of purifying selection and adaptive reversion in human gut bacteria, and uncover evidence for widespread weak selection at a large fraction of protein-coding sites. Our findings show that horizontal gene transfer can be an important factor in shaping genome-wide patterns of selective constraint, and raise new questions about the effectiveness of natural selection in complex bacterial populations.

title: Does perturbed adaptive myelination contribute to cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease?
content:
by Charles ffrench-Constant

The consequences of oligodendrocyte involvement in Alzheimer’s disease are poorly understood. Could a key role of gray-matter oligodendrocytes—activity-dependent adaptive myelination to sustain changes in activity—be perturbed, leading to cognitive loss? The consequences of oligodendrocyte involvement in Alzheimer’s disease are poorly understood. This Perspective suggests that activity-dependent adaptive myelination, a key role of grey-matter oligodendrocytes, could be perturbed, leading to cognitive loss.

title: The Cryptococcus neoformans titanide is a pathogenic cell type that arises from typical yeast cells in response to host conditions
content:
by Abigail M. Potton, Iana Kalinina, Gordon D. Brown, Maria Makarova, Sandra Catania, Dora E. Corzo-Leon, Elizabeth R. Ballou

Fungal morphogenesis is a major driver of disease outcome. For the opportunistic fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans, extreme morphological heterogeneity within the lung environment drives dissemination, immune evasion, and drug resistance. One such cell type is the small, oval, titanide (2–4 µm). This poorly understood cell type is prevalent in lung histology as well as host-relevant in vitro conditions. In conditions that generate cellular heterogeneity, titanides comprise 4%–10% of cells 24 hours post-induction and by 72 hours are the dominant cell type. Despite their prevalence and the significance of cryptococcal morphogenesis for virulence, key questions pertaining to their origin, fate, and underlying biology remain unstudied. Using TEM, SEM, and fluorescence microscopy we demonstrate that titanides display distinct morphological features; they possess thin cell walls, single birth scars, and capsules, with reduced Pathogen-Associated Molecular Pattern exposure and altered distribution. These features distinguish titanides from previously described C. neoformans ‘small cells’ such as in vivo seed cells (6 µm, high cell-wall mannan content) and micro cells (round, <1 μm, with thick cell walls) among others. Using microfluidics, we reveal that titanides arise from yeast-like ‘typical’ mothers, highlighting the morphological plasticity of typical cells in host-relevant conditions. Upon birth, titanides have compact nuclei and do not immediately proliferate, but transfer to fresh media results in rapid swelling and cell division. Consistent with this, titanides are more resistant to some cell wall/membrane stressors and are an effective infectious propagule in a murine model. Together, these findings establish a definition and essential characterisation of the titanide cell type and provide new insight into a key player in C. neoformans cell biology and pathogenesis.

title: Synaptic vesicle undocking induces low-frequency depression
content: Synaptic depression is often interpreted as reflecting depletion of the readily releasable pool (RRP) following exocytosis. Such a mechanism predicts little or no depression at low stimulation frequency, as RRP replenishment should then offset the loss of vesicles by exocytosis. Nevertheless, in several types of mammalian central synapses, repetitive presynaptic stimulation at low frequency (<5 Hz) elicits synaptic depression (low-frequency depression or LFD). In the present work, we count the number of synaptic vesicles released at individual active zones to study the RRP and its replenishment during LFD. Contrary to depletion models of synaptic depression, we find that LFD does not depend on previous SV consumption. We find that LFD displays a long recovery time course (tens of seconds) when challenged by isolated stimulations but is immediately reversed by a high-frequency train. We suggest that LFD results from undocking, a shift between two classes of synaptic vesicles organized sequentially inside the RRP (replacement vs. docked vesicles) in favor of the upstream (replacement) state. To explain the dependence of LFD recovery on stimulation frequency, we propose that, while undocking is apparent hundreds of milliseconds after a stimulation, calcium-dependent docking takes only a couple of milliseconds. Consistent with the undocking model, we find that double presynaptic stimulations alleviate LFD as they favor vesicular docking and RRP replenishment. Finally, we expand our model to explain how stimulation frequency shapes short-term synaptic depression, changing from depression at low frequency to a facilitation-depression sequence at medium- or high-frequency trains.

title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG
content: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

title: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain
content: Hormones mediate inter-organ signaling, which is crucial in orchestrating diverse behaviors and physiological processes, including sleep and activity, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. The pars intercerebralis and pars lateralis in insects represent major hubs that contain neurosecretory cells (NSCs) that produce various peptide hormones. To obtain insight into how hormonal signaling is regulated, we have characterized the synaptic connectome of NSCs in the adult Drosophila brain. Identification of neurons providing inputs to multiple NSC classes implicates diuretic hormone 44-expressing NSCs as a major coordinator of physiology and behavior. Surprisingly, despite most NSCs having dendrites in the subesophageal zone (primary taste processing center), inputs from peripheral gustatory neurons to NSCs are largely indirect. We also deciphered pathways via which diverse olfactory inputs are relayed to NSCs. Using an influence metric, based on a linear dynamical systems approach, we identify enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity compared to other sensory modalities. Further, our analyses revealed substantial inputs from brain descending neurons to NSCs, suggesting that descending neurons regulate both endocrine and motor output to synchronize physiological changes with appropriate behaviors. In contrast to NSC inputs, synaptic output from NSCs is sparse and mostly mediated by corazonin NSCs. We show that both corazonin-expressing NSCs and their downstream synaptic partner DNg27 influence egg-laying. We additionally explore putative paracrine interconnectivity between NSC classes and peptide hormone pathways from NSCs to peripheral tissues by analyzing single-cell transcriptomic datasets. Our comprehensive characterization of the Drosophila neurosecretory network connectome provides a platform to understand complex hormonal networks and how they orchestrate animal behaviors and physiology.

title: Dry pebble rain could have delivered water to Earth through hydrogen reduction of iron oxide
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02138-3

Much of the water on Earth could have been produced from dry silicate pebbles falling through the hot, hydrogen-rich primordial atmosphere as the planet formed. High-temperature experiments in streams of pure hydrogen demonstrate that the reduction of iron oxide in the silicates can produce water vapour in minutes or hours, and suggest that water production on Earth-sized exoplanets should be widespread.

title: An abrupt shift towards a hotter and drier climate regime in the Western Eurasian Steppe
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02125-8

The Western Eurasian Steppe has undergone an abrupt and persistent transition to a hotter and drier summer climate that exceeds the range of natural variability, driven by external climate forcing and amplified by internal variability and land–atmosphere feedbacks, according to observations and Earth system model simulations.

title: Family matters in the root microbiota
content:
Nature Microbiology, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02507-z

The root microbiota remains an untapped resource for sustainable agriculture — resolving its recruitment cues is a research priority for moving towards translational applications. Family-conserved functional repertoires emerge as building blocks of the root microbiota in distinct plants, opening new avenues for the rational manipulation of biological interactions at the root–soil continuum.

title: A conditional upper-bound design map for rhodopsin-augmented electro microbial CO2-to-biomass conversion
content: The value of rhodopsin proton pumps as light harvesters in electro-microbial CO2-to-biomass conversion depends on molecular photophysics, pathway energetics and reactor light delivery. We couple these scales for Cupriavidus necator, comparing Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) and reductive glycine (rGlyP) assimilation. The model predicts a 17.9% dark rGlyP yield advantage, close to 16.5% measured in chemostats. At 568 nm, 100 PPFD and 45% membrane occupancy, light-derived ATP raises yield by 17% for rGlyP and 14% for CBB. Charging CO2 capture and formate electrosynthesis, a retinal-only reactor reaches 3.29% efficiency versus 2.56% in the dark. A carotenoid antenna raises this to 3.52% at the model-derived 70% transfer estimate and helps in 93.2% of uncertainty samples, but lowers efficiency at the thermodynamic limit by diverting photons from photovoltaics. Point-source CO2 cuts the relative light benefit from 38% to 8%. Rhodopsin is therefore most useful when upstream formate is energy-intensive, not as a general efficiency boost.

title: Decision-relevant measurement for precision microbiome interventions
content: Human gut microbiome studies often rely on stool, despite increasing evidence that it incompletely represents the spatially heterogeneous intestinal ecosystem. Whether this loss of spatial detail matters for downstream intervention decisions is largely unresolved. We treat compositional reconstruction and decision preservation as separate objectives. Using 16 matched recovery events from 11 participants, each containing stool and four intended regional capsule measurements, we aggregated amplicon sequence variants into 11 prespecified taxonomic and functional proxy guilds. We evaluated models that reconstruct stool from regional measurements by nested leave one participant out validation under complementary compositional geometries. We then assessed decision preservation through three spatial proxy states and measurement induced decision loss (MIDL) across normalized binary intervention thresholds. Multi region CLR ridge and Aitchison models combining regional measurements with a population reference had the lowest point estimate Aitchison errors, but evidence that either outperformed the population Aitchison center was not retained after multiplicity correction. Rankings changed under total variation and after guild amalgamation; at the coarser resolution, the primary ordering showed a small, uncertain reversal that was sensitive to zero handling. The model with the lowest compositional error did not have the lowest MIDL curve calibration error. Population centers closely reproduced the nearly uninformative MIDL curves of observed stool while retaining little individualized regional information. These findings show that reconstruction, decision preservation, and calibration to observed stool decision loss answer different questions. Evaluation of microbiome measurement strategies should therefore treat compositional geometry, biological representation, and the downstream decision task as parts of the estimand.

title: The Human Gut Cell Atlas v1.0: A Unified, Community-BuiltReference of Cellular Diversity Across the Gut
content: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have transformed our understanding of cellular diversity in the human intestine, but differences in anatomical sampling, experimental processing and cell-type nomenclature limit comparison across datasets. Here, we present the Human Gut Cell Atlas (HGCA) V1, a community-curated reference of 944,390 healthy and disease-adjacent intestinal cells from 502 samples, 265 donors and 24 landmark studies, linked to detailed anatomical, clinical, and technical metadata. As this metadata is of critical importance to human biology, we developed MetaManager, an open source data management framework for standardized metadata collection and tracking. A five-level consensus taxonomy resolves 94 homeostatic cell identities and enables transferrable, high-resolution annotation of new gut datasets. By assembling cell identity, sampling metadata, and independent spatial validation, intestinal segment and radial tissue depth were revealed to systematically shape cellular composition and transcriptional state, enabling inference of the presence of sampling-dependent tissue niches, including lymphoid follicles. Reference mapping accurately and rapidly recovered cohort-level Crohn's disease and treatment signatures without de novo annotation, while mapping human intestinal organoids quantified cell-type-specific identity, regional specification, maturation, and transcriptional fidelity to native tissue. The HGCA V1 provides a standardized cellular, anatomical coordinate, and metadata system for reproducible, high-quality analysis of intestinal biology across healthy tissue, disease-associated remodelling, and experimental models, providing a continuously evolving community reference for cumulative discovery in human intestinal biology.

title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
content: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.

title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
content: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.

title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
content: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.

title: Distribution and dynamics of Vibrio spp. and pathogen sequences among microhabitats and monsoon seasons in Singapore's coastal waters
content: Marine infections are rising in temperate regions due in part to a warming climate. However, comparatively little is known about drivers of marine pathogen dynamics in the tropics where temperatures are high year-round. Vibrio bacteria are ubiquitous in both temperate and tropical marine environments, and many are important pathogens of marine organisms and humans. Here, we sampled an equatorial monsoonal site, the Singapore Strait, over 18 months and applied amplicon sequencing (16s rRNA V6-8 region) to three particle size fractions, qPCR quantitation of Vibrio spp., and generalized linear modelling with environmental variables to understand the factors that structure the Vibrio assemblage. We found that Vibrios represented the highest proportion of pathogen-related DNA sequences, with an assemblage composition influenced by microhabitats (size fractions) and monsoon seasons. Vibrio sequences were dominated by ASVs with highest identity to V. xuii, V. rotiferianus and V. caribbeanicus, and including ASVs matching agents of human disease in Singapore - V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus, and V. furnissii. Vibrio qPCR abundance was lowest in the largest size fraction (10-150 m), following planktonic DNA trends, even though pathogen-related sequences, including Vibrio, were enriched in this fraction. Temperature was a significant predictor of overall Vibrio abundance, but its effect was no longer significant after adjustment for monsoons, suggesting that the temperature association may reflect broader seasonal dynamics. Instead, effects of chlorophyll, ammonia, nitrate and suspended solids were more consistent within seasons. Furthermore, free-living and particle-associated Vibrios responded differently to environmental changes, suggesting that partitioning into microspatial habitats may lead to differences in their environmental sensitivity.

title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
content: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.

title: Pulling water from a stone: subaerial biofilm water dynamics on porous solid materials
content: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) are microbial communities that colonize air exposed surfaces in both natural and engineered environments, forming an interface between the atmosphere and the substrate. Often water availability is crucial for their metabolic activity and survival. While precipitation may contribute to SAB hydration, the dynamic processes of evaporation and condensation - closely linked to fluctuating temperature and humidity conditions - can be key determinants of water availability and they constitute the main focus of this study. We present a model connecting the water-related dynamics in an SAB, its surrounding ambient air and underlying stone/masonry. A central feature of the model is the increased water affinity of the SAB in comparison to the stone pore network. Based on thermodynamic principles, the model captures changes in liquid water content and availability by accounting for the evaporation and condensation at liquid-gas interfaces through gradients in water chemical potential. It accounts for the SAB's capacity to delay water loss by drawing water from substrate material pores to compensate for atmospheric evaporation. The proposed model is compared to prior experimental observations of water transport in limestone samples with and without SAB. Additional numerical simulations under variable environmental conditions demonstrate how permeability of the substrate layer may influence SAB water activity, and how the presence or absence of an SAB might affect water content within stone/masonry.

title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from  Escherichia coli  identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
content: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.

title: Genome-wide CRISPRi mapping of mycobacteriophage interaction determinants in Mycobacterium smegmatis mc2155
content: Bacteriophages are highly specific predators of bacterial hosts, but the molecular mechanisms governing their entry across the structurally complex mycobacterial cell envelope remain poorly defined. Utilizing a genome-wide CRISPR interference library in the model organism Mycobacterium smegmatis against a phylogenetically representative collection of 70 mycobacteriophages, we mapped the functional architecture of host susceptibility determinants. This parallelized genetic screen revealed a spatial continuum of infection requirements spanning from outer leaflet surface structures down to deep cytoplasmic machinery. The four major outer membrane Mycobacterium smegmatis porins (Msp) emerged as the dominant candidate receptor family for 46 diverse phages, representing the first protein receptors identified within this group. Interrogating the asymmetric outer bilayer also implicated cell envelope glycolipids as candidate receptors for 14 phages, resolving into glycopeptidolipid sub-lineages. Beneath the mycomembrane, arabinogalactan functions as a candidate secondary receptor for 5 phages, while the inner membrane lipid transporter MmpL11 and the global nucleoid-associated protein Lsr2 represent determinant factors for 14 and 31 phages respectively. While physical deletions of major porins trigger spontaneous regulatory pathways that upregulate silent backup paralogues, acute transcriptional knockdowns circumvent suppressor accumulation, revealing unmasked single-gene dependencies. Structural analysis demonstrated that host determinant usage decouples entirely from whole-genome viral phylogeny, indicating that standard phylogenetic groupings fail to predict surface recognition profiles. Ultimately, mapping this host interactome reveals an evolutionary strategy where phages target highly redundant or abundant host machinery to exploit fixed physiological liabilities, presenting a robust molecular blueprint for the rational engineering of escape-resistant therapeutic phage cocktails.

title: Metabolic reorganization shapes the dynamics of a water kefir microbial community
content: Microbial fermentations emerge from the collective activity of interacting species whose relative abundances, metabolic functions, and environmental constraints continuously change over time. Water kefir provides a tractable model to investigate how multispecies communities coordinate their metabolic activities during fermentation. Here, we combined time-resolved community profiling, physicochemical measurements, metabolite quantification, and controlled co-culture assays to characterize the dynamics of a water kefir consortium comprising 19 detected microbial species. Our results reveal that water kefir fermentation is not adequately described as a simple succession of independently acting microbial groups. Instead, the community undergoes a reproducible reorganization of its collective metabolism around 20 h of fermentation. This transition marks a shift from an early regime characterized by the accumulation of soluble sugars and ethanol to a later regime dominated by enhanced sugar consumption and lactate production. Controlled interaction assays further showed that bacterial partners can alter carbon-use behaviour in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, highlighting the capacity of interspecies interactions to reshape metabolic phenotypes within the consortium. Together, these results support an ecological view of water kefir fermentation in which community-wide metabolic reorganization emerges from the interplay between microbial interactions, resource availability, and environmental change.

title: Maintenance of restriction-modification system diversity creates pan-immunity
content: Bacterial antiviral defense systems are highly diverse and unevenly distributed across populations, such that different strains carry distinct immune repertoires that together form a pan-immune system. Restriction-modification (RM) systems are the most abundant bacterial defense systems and exemplify this architecture, exhibiting remarkable diversity in structure, function, specificity, and efficacy. How and why such diversity is maintained, why weaker systems are not outcompeted, and whether diversity provides benefits beyond protection of individual cells remain unclear. Here, we experimentally tracked bacteria and phages across populations differing in RM diversity. We find no consistent evidence of a trade-off between defense strength and host fitness. Instead, we identify a trade-off between defense strength and horizontal transferability: stronger RM systems are less able to spread between strains, likely because factors that increase defense strength also increase toxicity risk upon transfer to unmethylated hosts. These weaker yet more mobile systems may therefore act as more accessible pan-immune components that bacterial populations can acquire in response to shifting parasite pressures. Furthermore, we show RM systems experience negative frequency-dependent selection, such that common specificities are more readily overcome by phages while rare ones remain protective, causing the benefits of potent systems to erode as they spread. Together, these dynamics maintain RM diversity and explain why weaker systems persist alongside stronger ones. Finally, we show that population-level RM diversity generates collective protection by constraining the emergence of RM-escaping phages and limiting the invasion of bacterial surface mutants that avoid phage adsorption, providing experimental support for the pan-immune model.

title: Planting set-up and local environmental conditions affect outcomes in tropical agricultural restoration
content: 1. Fine-scale environmental metrics, including spatial configuration and identity of surrounding plants, can strongly influence plant survival and ecosystem functioning. However, tropical restoration projects rarely test their role. Within the Riparian Ecosystem Restoration in Tropical Agriculture (RERTA) Project, located within oil palm plantations in Indonesia, we investigated how the spatial configuration and position of enrichment-planted trees influenced restoration outcomes within actively restored riparian margins. 2. We compared the enrichment plantings' response to fine-scale spatial conditions, either planted with conspecific (same-species) or heterospecific (mixed-species) neighbours for six planted tree species (Peronema canescens, Shorea leprosula, Alstonia scholaris, Artocarpus integer, Calophyllum inophyllum, and Albizia chinensis), in restoration areas with mature oil palms either left in place (shaded) or removed (unshaded). We also tested whether restoration outcomes varied with position within the margin (river, middle, or edge). We measured plantings response as seedling survival and height (monitored over eight years) for all six species of trees. 3. We also carried out more detailed observation on multiple ecosystem functions associated with focal trees of three of the species (Peronema canescens, Alstonia scholaris, and Albizia chinensis), measuring differences by planting configuration and distance to river edge. Functions measured included: herbivore predation, leaf herbivory, litterfall, soil chemical properties (organic carbon, cation exchange capacity, total nitrogen, and phosphorus), and soil physical properties (bulk density, aggregate stability, friable soil content, and A-horizon depth). 4. Survival and height did not differ between conspecific and heterospecific neighbours, but did with position within the riparian margin, but only when analysed by treatment and time. Planting configuration and position influenced ecosystem functions; heterospecific plantings had greater soil aggregate stability and higher ant densities, while increasing distance from the river was associated with lower arthropod abundance and herbivory but greater predation. 5. Our findings demonstrate that planting outcomes are strongly context-dependent, with local seedling configurations, position within the riparian margin, and restoration treatment interacting to influence restoration success and local ecological conditions. Our findings provide experimental results to inform planting strategies and restoration protocols in agricultural landscapes.

title: Precocious reproduction in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi is modulated by conspecific density and food availability
content: Precocious reproduction, prior to the acquisition of the final adult morphology, occurs in a variety of animals and represents a distinct life-history strategy with important consequences for growth and survival. Larval reproduction is far rarer and usually restricted to groups that go through metamorphosis. In ctenophores, Carl Chun described dissogeny more than 130 years ago, a distinctive life-history pattern involving larval and adult reproductive periods separated by gonadal regression. Yet, the potential plasticity of larval reproduction in ctenophores remains unresolved. Here, we developed a method to follow and quantify reproductive output in Mnemiopsis leidyi larvae and tested environmental factors that may regulate precocious reproduction. We found that conspecific density strongly influences its onset: low-density, well-fed animals can bypass reproduction at the cydippid stage and develop rapidly into the lobed form, whereas higher density promotes precocious reproduction. Food availability and associated growth rate also contribute but cannot alone explain the observed differences. Once reproduction is established, however, high conspecific density suppresses reproductive output, an effect reproduced by exposure to seawater incubated with high M. leidyi densities, consistent with water-borne chemical communication. Salinity and light conditions further modulate spawning. Together, our results reveal substantial environmental plasticity in precocious reproduction in M. leidyi, reconcile long-standing contradictory observations of ctenophore development, and highlight how environmental cues can reshape reproductive life-history transitions.

title: From Bad to Worse: Carryover Effects Alter Responses to Multiple Stressors
content: Ecological responses to environmental stressors are increasingly shaped by interactions among anthropogenic and climatic drivers, yet the influence of prior exposure history on subsequent stress responses remains poorly integrated into multiple stressor ecology. Using the blue mussel (Mytilus edulis) as a model system, we experimentally tested whether prior exposure to environmental nanoplastics modifies responses to subsequent stressors, including copper contamination, nutrient enrichment, and salinity fluctuations, individually and in combination. Nanoplastic pre-exposure reduced survival across subsequent treatments and altered stressor interaction outcomes at the community level, shifting responses toward synergistic effects that amplified metabolic costs. These results demonstrate that exposure history can modify both the magnitude and direction of multi-stressor effects, with consequences extending beyond individual performance to ecosystem functioning. By incorporating temporal exposure dynamics into multiple stressor research, our study highlights how ecological responses to global change depend not only on the identity and intensity of stressors, but also on prior environmental conditions shaping subsequent organismal and ecosystem health status and responses.

title: When does heterogeneity average out in coarse-grained ecological communities?
content: Ecological coarse-graining of individuals or species into aggregate variables, such as total biomass or regional abundance, is common practice, yet differences among species can still influence aggregate dynamics. We propose a metric for quantifying this irreducible dynamical heterogeneity. For small fluctuations near a stable equilibrium, we compare the aggregate fluctuation spectrum of the full dynamical system with that of the best Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model having the same dimension as the aggregate. The remaining spectral mismatch quantifies the dynamical effects of hidden differences that the fitted aggregate model cannot capture. For weakly interacting random community models at fixed collective interaction strength, we show that increasing species richness can either reduce or increase this heterogeneity, depending on how species interact. Our framework helps understand when ecological and evolutionary differences average out versus when their dynamical effects persist.

title: Simple soil eDNA sampling reveals terrestrial mammal diversity in the Central Kalahari and highlights waterholes as sampling hotspots
content: Remote and vast ecosystems present a challenge for biodiversity monitoring. The Central Kalahari Game Reserve in Botswana is one such ecosystem spanning 52,800 km2, a mosaic of fossilized rivers, clay pans, semi-arid sand dunes, scrub, and woodland. It is one of the last remaining untouched wildernesses in the world and hosts unique biodiversity, including populations of threatened mammals. Due to its extreme arid environment, size, and inaccessibility, surveying biodiversity across the reserve is both logistically and technically difficult. Here we demonstrate that a low-effort approach of sampling soil across the reserve is an efficient way to rapidly assess the terrestrial mammal biodiversity using eDNA metabarcoding. We found that eDNA from soil near waterholes performed better at capturing local biodiversity than soil from roads. eDNA metabarcoding detected 38 mammal species, 15 bird species and two amphibians and a simultaneously conducted camera trapping study detected 29 mammal species. eDNA was particularly powerful for detecting small-bodied taxa, including murids, mongooses and bats, which were largely missed by camera traps, while camera trapping was aimed at and performed well for detecting felids. Mammal species that had a higher activity nearby eDNA sampling points (i.e., a higher number of camera trapping recordings nearby) had a higher probability of being detected via eDNA. We propose that simple soil collection for eDNA metabarcoding, particularly close to animal congregation points such as savanna waterholes, offers a practical, scalable and cost-effective strategy for DNA-based biomonitoring in large, remote areas such those in Southern Africa.

title: Coarse Woody Debris of Mixed Tree Species Overrides Soil Matrix Constraints on Microbial Richness and Abundance in an Ancient Broad-Leaved Forest
content: The mechanisms by which coarse woody debris (CWD) affects soil microbial diversity across different spatial scales and forest disturbance regimes remain poorly understood. This study investigated the impact of CWD from multiple tree species on forest floor bacterial and fungal communities under varying landscape-scale conditions, specifically comparing old-growth forests situated on Phaozems and Retisols with mass-windthrow areas located on loamy Retisols and sandy Podzols. We analyzed both chemical compound and metagenomic profiles of 63 CWD-associated soil samples collected from the Kaluzhskie Zaseki Nature Reserve (European part of Russia). High-throughput Illumina sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and the ITS region was used to profile both bacterial and fungal communities, respectively. Scale-dependent diversity patterns and taxonomic accumulation were assessed using GLM, NMDS, dbRDA, and iNEXT frameworks. Our findings revealed a profound spatial decoupling in forest floor microbial communities, where a localized reduction in alpha-diversity under CWD drove a sharp increase in landscape-scale gamma-diversity. While standard soil physicochemical properties rigidly dictated baseline matrix richness, CWD operated as a powerful micro-environmental hotspot overriding these constraints. Deadwood inputs filtered out dominant matrix-associated taxa, creating highly specialized micro-refugia characterized by high compositional dispersion. This niche selection was particularly pronounced beneath Quercus logs on Phaozems and Retisols. Furthermore, post-windthrow microbial responses were heavily filtered by wood traits and baseline soil textures. On loamy Retisols within the windthrow mosaic, this breakaway dynamic was highly taxon-specific: while Acer and Fraxinus CWD triggered partitioned, site-specific hotspot dynamics yielding an exceptionally large pool of unique ASVs for bacteria, the distinct enrichment for fungal communities was primarily driven by Ulmus CWD and log-free windthrow areas. Ultimately, iNEXT accumulation profiles confirmed that deadwood does not merely multiply common soil taxa, but enriches the forest landscape by injecting critical beta-level heterogeneity into the soil matrix. These insights emphasize the role of diverse CWD retention in buffering forest microbiomes against large-scale environmental disturbances across heterogeneous soil landscapes.

title: Beyond Environmental Matching: Maternal Effects Depend on Offspring Environmental Complexity and Fitness Traits
content: The consequences of maternal effects for offspring fitness can depend on the environmental conditions offspring encounter and the fitness traits considered. We used a transgenerational experiment in Daphnia magna to test how maternal exposure to warming and elevated salinity influenced offspring survival, reproduction and body size across matching, mismatching and multiple-stressor environments. Maternal exposure to salinity enhanced offspring survival under matching salinity, and benefits extended to mismatching environments. In contrast, maternal exposure to warming provided no survival benefit under matching warming and reduced survival in mismatching environments, while accelerating reproduction across contexts. Multiple-stressor conditions revealed pronounced maternal effects, while contrasting responses across survival, reproduction and body size showed that benefits to one fitness trait did not extend to others. Our findings demonstrate that environmental matching alone is insufficient to predict maternal effects, whose consequences depend on offspring environmental complexity and the fitness trait considered.
